drivingQuestion: Are a limb and flesh that hang partially severed from an animal treated as attached or as detached for the laws of impurity?
outcomeNote: A mishna recording two parallel disputes of R' Meir and R' Shimon without resolving either; the gemara takes them up.

segments.he: מַתְנִי׳ הָאֵבֶר וְהַבָּשָׂר הַמְדוּלְדָּלִין בַּבְּהֵמָה, מְטַמְּאִין טוּמְאַת אֳכָלִין בִּמְקוֹמָן, וּצְרִיכִין הֶכְשֵׁר.
segments.en: «MISHNA:» «The limb» of an animal, with flesh, sinews, and bones, «and the flesh» of an animal, «that were» partially severed and remain «hanging from the animal» do not have the halakhic status of a limb severed from a living animal, which imparts impurity like an unslaughtered carcass, or of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure, respectively. If one had intent to eat the limb or the flesh, the limb or flesh becomes impure if it comes in contact with a source of impurity, and they «impart impurity as food» to other foods and liquids, although they remain «in their place» attached to the animal. «But» in order for them to become impure, «they need» to be «rendered susceptible» to impurity through contact with one of the seven liquids that facilitate susceptibility.

segments.he: נִשְׁחֲטָה הַבְּהֵמָה – הוּכְשְׁרוּ בְּדָמֶיהָ, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר. רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹמֵר: לֹא הוּכְשְׁרוּ.
segments.en: If «the animal was slaughtered,» although this act of slaughter does not render it permitted for consumption by a Jew (see 73b), the limb and the flesh «were» thereby «rendered susceptible» to impurity by coming in contact «with the blood of» the slaughtered animal, as blood is one of the seven liquids; this is «the statement of Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Shimon says: They were not rendered susceptible» to impurity through the animal’s own blood; they are rendered susceptible only once they have been wet with another liquid.

segments.he: מֵתָה הַבְּהֵמָה – הַבָּשָׂר צָרִיךְ הֶכְשֵׁר, הָאֵבֶר מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר מִן הַחַי, וְאֵינוֹ מְטַמֵּא מִשּׁוּם אֵבֶר נְבֵלָה – דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר, וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן מְטַהֵר.
segments.en: If «the animal died» without slaughter, «the» hanging «flesh needs» to be «rendered susceptible» to impurity in order to become impure, as its halakhic status is that of flesh severed from a living animal, which is ritually pure and does not have the status of an unslaughtered carcass. «The» hanging «limb imparts impurity as a limb» severed «from a living» animal «but does not impart impurity as the limb of» an unslaughtered «carcass;» this is «the statement of Rabbi Meir. And Rabbi Shimon deems» the limb «ritually pure.»

moves.summary: the mishna rules that a partially severed limb and flesh impart food impurity in their place and need to be rendered susceptible
R' Meir supplies how they are rendered susceptible: the blood of the slaughter does it
moves.about: the ruling that the blood of the slaughtered animal renders the hanging limb and flesh susceptible to impurity

moves.summary: R' Shimon denies that the animal's own blood renders them susceptible
moves.about: whether the blood of the animal's own slaughter renders the partially severed limb and flesh susceptible to impurity

moves.summary: R' Meir rules the parallel case of an animal that died: the flesh needs hekhsher, the limb imparts impurity as a limb from a living animal only
moves.about: the ruling that after the animal dies the hanging limb imparts impurity as a limb from a living animal but not as a limb of a carcass

moves.summary: R' Shimon deems the hanging limb pure
moves.about: whether the limb left hanging on an animal that died imparts impurity as a limb from a living animal or is wholly pure
